lines.text: Christ on our lives, of Him who wishes to release us from our
self-concern by bestowing these mercies upon us. And we
shall understand too that what was bestowed on us was not
bestowed to make us linger over it but to make us look
forward to the future, that it might bear fruit in the future.
The purpose of the gift was to make us more mature and
capable for the carrying out of future tasks. In a twofold way.
Firstly everything that has come our way should inspire us
with courage and strength to meet what the future holds,
should fill us with aspiration to live a nobler and purer life,
and should make us ready both for action and sacrifice. But
in such a way that we never forget that "in our own strength
we can accomplish nothing, soon we stumble and fall".
What we now have and are, is His gift, and also what we shall
become will be His gift. And our readiness for action and
sacrifice will only be maintained and come to good effect if
it implies readiness to live by the gift of His grace, to allow
His grace, to allow Him to act upon us and within us, as He
wills; and this means readiness to abandon ourselves as it
were to that void in which there is no support and no
security, in which we are held only by the grip of Him who in
our recent past has thrust with power and grace into our
lives.
III
But perhaps there are some among us who do not dare to
say that they can detect the grip of Christ upon them in the
experiences which the term now ending has brought.
Perhaps there are some who do not look back with glad and
grateful hearts, but with disillusionment and dismay. What
has the term brought? Increase of knowledge perhaps, but
knowledge without inspiration or power. Perhaps
insight, yes, but a painful insight, the discovery of the
insecurity of what seemed secure. Doubt about what seemed
certain and in consequence doubt about the meaning and
worthwhileness of our work. Or did the term bring neglected
opportunities and wasted hours? Doubt about ourselves?
